Overview

Colombo as a Business Centre

Colombo is Sri Lanka's commercial capital and financial centre. Although the administrative capital moved to neighbouring Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, the President's House, many ministries and the Supreme Court remain in Colombo. The city proper counted about 753,000 residents in the 2011 census, within a metropolitan area commonly estimated at more than five million. The Western Province around it accounts for a large share of national output and most industrial value added. Colombo is home to the head offices of the country's major diversified groups, including John Keells Holdings, Aitken Spence, Hemas Holdings and Cargills, and its port is a leading transshipment hub for the Indian Ocean.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Colombo because so much of Sri Lanka's corporate ownership, trade finance and investment decision-making is concentrated there. Acquirers and lenders want to understand diversified family groups whose holdings span listed and private companies. Shipping, logistics and commodity businesses need to know who controls the agents, freight forwarders and traders moving cargo through a port where most volume is transshipment. Port City Colombo, built on reclaimed land beside the old Fort district and governed by its own commission, is drawing offshore investors and service providers whose backgrounds deserve scrutiny. Creditors and counsel in disputes after the country's 2022 economic crisis also need reliable facts about counterparties and their assets.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Colombo

01

Conglomerate and family group mapping

Mapping the listed and private companies, cross-holdings, directors and related parties of Colombo-headquartered diversified groups before an acquisition, joint venture or financing, so investors understand where control actually sits and which group entities carry litigation, regulatory or reputational exposure.

02

Transshipment and trade counterparty checks

Researching shipping agents, freight forwarders, traders and consignees connected to cargo moving through the Port of Colombo, including ownership, adverse media and sanctions screening, to help clients assess trade-based money laundering, misdeclaration and diversion risk on transshipped goods.

03

Port City investor due diligence

Background research on developers, authorised persons, offshore companies and their promoters seeking business or property in Port City Colombo, covering ownership, source-of-wealth indicators, disputes and political exposure, for co-investors, lenders and tenants assessing who they are dealing with.

04

Post-crisis asset and creditor research

Identifying assets, related companies and transfers of Colombo-based debtors and guarantors after Sri Lanka's 2022 economic crisis, assembling publicly documented facts that counsel can use in restructuring negotiations, recovery proceedings or enforcement of judgments and awards.

05

Procurement and infrastructure partners

Reviewing contractors, consultants and local partners on port, urban development and other public projects in Colombo, including links to officials, prior disputes and debarments, to help sponsors and lenders manage bribery and conflict-of-interest risk under the 2023 anti-corruption framework.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Colombo

Courts sitting in Colombo

Colombo is the seat of the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka and of the Commercial High Court, which hears commercial disputes above a prescribed value. District courts and magistrates' courts in the city deal with civil and criminal matters at first instance. Because the country's most significant commercial litigation is concentrated in Colombo, court records there are a key source when assessing a counterparty's disputes, though retrieving filings generally requires local counsel.

Port City Colombo Economic Commission

The Colombo Port City Economic Commission Act No. 11 of 2021 established a commission that licenses authorised persons, registers offshore companies, regulates investment and land leases and acts as a single window for investors in the special economic zone. Foreign exchange regulations issued in 2022 govern Port City investment accounts. A proposal announced in 2023 to develop the zone as a Colombo Financial Zone with offshore jurisdiction had not been confirmed as enacted in our research.

Port City dispute resolution

The Port City framework provides for an International Commercial Dispute Resolution Centre offering conciliation, mediation, adjudication and arbitration, and commentators note that disputes within the zone are expected to be resolved through it. Courts are also directed to give priority to civil and commercial matters connected to Port City business. Alongside the Sri Lanka National Arbitration Centre and the ICLP Arbitration Centre, this gives Colombo several dispute forums.

Port City incentives and currency rules

Businesses in Port City Colombo can receive extensive tax exemptions, with businesses of strategic importance eligible for incentives of up to 40 years, and many transactions are conducted in designated foreign currency. These features make it important to establish who ultimately benefits from Port City entities and how funds move in and out, particularly where offshore companies and nominee arrangements are involved.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Colombo

For matters touching Colombo, TDSC begins by defining the decision the client faces, whether that is an investment alongside a diversified group, a trade relationship through the port or a Port City counterparty, and then identifies the relevant sources: Registrar of Companies filings, Colombo Stock Exchange disclosures, Commercial High Court and other court records, Port City licensing information, English, Sinhala and Tamil media and international trade and sanctions data. Research is conducted from Nashville. Where court file retrieval, local enquiries or interviews are justified, TDSC coordinates with qualified Sri Lankan professionals and the client's Sri Lankan counsel. Personal data is collected only as the matter requires and handled with Sri Lanka's data protection rules in mind.

TDSC has no office in Colombo. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Colombo: Frequently Asked Questions

Can you research a Colombo diversified group before we invest?

Yes. We map the group's listed and unlisted companies, directors, cross-holdings and related parties from registry filings, stock exchange disclosures and media, then review litigation, regulatory actions and reputation. We also look for related-party transactions and concentrations of control that may affect minority investors, and flag where private holdings cannot be fully documented from public sources.

What does the Port City Colombo regime mean for due diligence?

Port City Colombo has its own commission, licensing of authorised persons, offshore company registration, foreign-currency rules and tax incentives under Act No. 11 of 2021. Diligence should confirm what licences a counterparty actually holds, who stands behind it and how it is funded, since incentives and offshore structures can attract parties seeking opacity.

Can you check freight forwarders and traders using the Port of Colombo?

We research ownership, registration, adverse media, litigation and sanctions screening results for agents, forwarders, traders and consignees, and look for inconsistencies in their stated business. Because much Colombo volume is transshipment, we pay attention to links with third countries and to signs of misdeclaration or diversion of goods.

Where are commercial disputes involving Colombo companies heard?

Significant commercial disputes are generally heard by the Commercial High Court in Colombo, with appeals to the Supreme Court, which also sits in the city. Arbitration is available through Colombo-based centres, and the Port City framework provides its own dispute resolution centre. We support counsel with factual research; we do not give legal advice.

Does TDSC have an office in Colombo?

No. TDSC is based in Nashville and has no office or staff in Colombo or elsewhere in Sri Lanka. Most of our work is desk-based research. Where on-the-ground steps are needed, we coordinate with qualified local professionals acting lawfully and with the client's Sri Lankan counsel, and we decline requests involving restricted records or covert methods.
